problem:
From top to bottom, fill in the blanks and hence complete the proof of the following statement using the axioms $[\text{A}1]-[\text{A}8]$ given below.

*Statement:*

*Given any $x\in V$, if $y$ is a vector such that $x+y=0$, then $y=-x.$* 

*Proof:*

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =0 &  & [\,\text{given}\,] \\ (x+y)+(-x) & =0+(-x) &  & [\,\text{add }-x\text{ to both sides}\,] \\ (y+x)+(-x) & =(-x)+0 &  & [\,\text{axiom A1}\,] \\ (y+x)+(-x) & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ y+(x+(-x)) & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ y+0 & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom A4}\,] \\ y & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom A3}\,]\end{aligned}
$$

The axioms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{[A1]}:x+y=y+x & \text{[A5]}:1\cdot x=x \\ \text{[A2]}:(x+y)+z=x+(y+z) & \text{[A6]}:\alpha (\beta x)=(\alpha \beta )x \\ \text{[A3]}:x+0=x & \text{[A7]}:(\alpha +\beta )x=\alpha x+\beta x \\ \text{[A4]}:x+(-x)=0 & \text{[A8]}:\alpha (x+y)=\alpha x+\alpha y\end{aligned}
$$

examples.knowledge_point: Proving Statements Using the Vector Space Axioms
examples.problem:
From top to bottom, fill in the blanks and hence complete the proof of the following statement using the axioms $[\textrm A1] - [\textrm A8]$ given below.

*Statement: *

*If $\mathbf{w}$ is a vector such that $\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{w}$, then $\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{0}.$* 

*Proof:*

$$
\begin{aligned}w+w & =w &  & [\,\text{given}\,] \\ (w+w)+(-w) & =w+(-w) &  & [\,\text{add [math]-\mathbf{w}[/math] to both sides}\,] \\ w+(w+(-w)) & =w+(-w) &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ w+0 & =0 &  & [\,\text{axiom A4}\,] \\ w & =0 &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,]\end{aligned}
$$

The axioms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{[A1]}:x+y=y+x & \text{[A5]}:1\cdot x=x \\ \text{[A2]}:(x+y)+z=x+(y+z) & \text{[A6]}:\alpha (\beta x)=(\alpha \beta )x \\ \text{[A3]}:x+0=x & \text{[A7]}:(\alpha +\beta )x=\alpha x+\beta x \\ \text{[A4]}:x+(-x)=0 & \text{[A8]}:\alpha (x+y)=\alpha x+\alpha y\end{aligned}
$$
examples.worked_solution:
Using the axioms of a vector space, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}w+w & =w &  & [\,\text{given}\,] \\ (w+w)+(-w) & =w+(-w) &  & [\,\text{add [math]-\mathbf{w}[/math] to both sides}\,] \\ w+(w+(-w)) & =w+(-w) &  & [\,\text{axiom [math]{\color{blue}\text{A2}}[/math]}\,] \\ w+0 & =0 &  & [\,\text{axiom A4}\,] \\ w & =0 &  & [\,\text{axiom [math]{\color{blue}\text{A3}}[/math]}\,]\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Let $J$ be the set of purely imaginary complex numbers, that is, complex numbers of the form  $ai,$ where  $a$ is a nonzero real number. Complete the following sentence: 

*$J$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to addition of complex numbers and scalar multiplication of a complex number by a real number) because $\text{_________}\,.$*
feedback.worked_solution:
The correct answer is as follows:

*$J$ is **not** a vector space (with respect to addition of complex numbers and scalar multiplication of a complex number by a real number) because **multiplication of $z\in J$ by real scalars is not closed.** *

For example, if $\alpha =0$ and $z=i,$ then $\alpha \cdot z=0\cdot i=0\notin J.$

On the other hand:

- Addition in $J$ is associative. $\,✓$

- Addition  in $J$ is commutative.  $\,✓$

- Addition and scalar multiplication in $J$ satisfy the distributive laws. $\,✓$

- If  $z\in J$ then $z=ai$ for some $a\in R.$ Hence, $-z=(-a)i\in J$   since $-a\in R.$ $\,✓$

submitted_fields.submitted_value: multiplication of $z\in J$ by real  scalars is not closed
